patient_name: OET role-play — new mother on the postnatal ward with sore nipples, thinking of stopping breastfeeding
chief_complaint: Support a first-time mother who has painful nipples and believes she does not have enough milk, while respecting her choice about feeding

team_brief.title: Breastfeeding support: first-time mother with sore nipples, ready to switch to formula
team_brief.patient: Ms Aisha Rahman, 27-year-old first-time mother; her daughter Maryam is 2 days old, born at full term by vaginal birth
team_brief.location: Postnatal ward, mid-morning; you are the nurse caring for Ms Rahman and her baby
team_brief.situation: Ms Rahman has been breastfeeding since the birth, but her nipples are sore and cracked and Maryam wants to feed very often, especially in the evening. She has just told you she is thinking of switching to formula because she does not think she has enough milk.
background: Uncomplicated pregnancy and birth. Maryam is healthy and was a normal birth weight.
Ms Rahman wanted to breastfeed before the birth.
Her mother-in-law, who is visiting, has suggested that the baby is hungry and needs a bottle.
current_status: You watched a feed this morning: Maryam was attached shallowly, mainly on the nipple, and Ms Rahman winced throughout.
Maryam has had the wet and dirty nappies expected for her age, and the baby check this morning was normal.
Ms Rahman is tired and tearful.
key_data: In the first days a baby's stomach is very small; the early milk (colostrum) comes in small amounts but is exactly what the baby needs. Milk usually increases over the next few days.
Feeding often — around 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, sometimes clustered in the evening — is normal and helps build the milk supply.
Sore, cracked nipples are most often caused by the baby not being attached deeply enough; changing position and attachment usually eases the pain.
Signs the baby is getting enough: regular wet and dirty nappies that increase over the first week, swallowing sounds during feeds, a settled baby after most feeds, and weight checks by the midwife.
Support: the infant feeding team can see her on the ward today; community peer supporters and the health visitor are available after discharge.
treatments: Already done: routine postnatal checks for mother and baby.
Pending: infant feeding team review if she agrees; baby's weight check in the coming days as per local routine.
team_brief.your_request: Find out what Ms Rahman is finding difficult, give her accurate information and practical help, and support whatever decision she makes about feeding.
must_include: Find out what Ms Rahman is finding difficult about breastfeeding and how she is feeling.
Reassure her that frequent feeding and small amounts of early milk (colostrum) are normal.
Explain how changing the baby's position and attachment can reduce nipple pain.
Explain how she can tell that her baby is getting enough milk.
Respect her decision about feeding and tell her about the support available.

kickoff_text: I don't think I can keep doing this. It really hurts, and she's hungry all the time — I just don't have enough milk for her.
persona_override: You are Aisha Rahman, a 27-year-old first-time mother on the postnatal ward. Your daughter Maryam is 2 days old and healthy. You are exhausted, tearful, and feel like you are failing. You really wanted to breastfeed, but your nipples are sore and cracked, Maryam feeds very often (especially in the evening), and you are convinced you do not have enough milk. Your specific worry, which you only say if the nurse asks how you are feeling or what is worrying you: your mother-in-law keeps saying the baby is starving, and you are afraid you are harming Maryam and that everyone will think you are a bad mother. Ground truth: pain is worst at the start of each feed and stays throughout; Maryam has had wet and dirty nappies as the midwife expected; she feeds about 10 times a day; you usually feed her sitting up in bed, cradled across your body, but you are not sure how to get her on properly; nobody has helped you with attachment since the first day; you have not given any formula yet. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words such as 'colostrum', 'latch', 'attachment', 'lactation' or 'supply and demand' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse jumps straight into breastfeeding instructions or pushes you to keep breastfeeding without asking how you feel, become more upset and bring up your worry more anxiously: 'But what if she's starving? My mother-in-law says she is.' If the nurse makes you feel judged or says you 'should' breastfeed, say quietly, 'So I'm a bad mother if I give her a bottle?' If the nurse acknowledges your feelings, reassures you about colostrum and frequent feeds, and explains the nappy signs, calm down gradually and ask a practical question: 'So how do I make it hurt less?' Accept an offer of help from the infant feeding team, and say you will try for another day or two — but only if the nurse has made it clear it is your choice. If asked to repeat how you will know she is getting enough, mention the nappies but forget the other signs. Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up: thank the nurse and say you feel a bit better.
learning_objectives: find out what the mother is finding difficult and how she is feeling
reassure that colostrum and frequent feeding are normal in the first days
explain in plain words how position and attachment can reduce nipple pain
explain the signs that the baby is getting enough milk such as wet and dirty nappies
respect the mother's choice about feeding without judgement
offer support from the infant feeding team and peer supporters
suggested_questions: It sounds like the last two days have been really hard. Can you tell me what's been the most difficult part, and how you're feeling about it?
What you're describing — Maryam wanting to feed very often, especially in the evening — is actually very normal at two days old. Her tummy is tiny, and your early milk is exactly what she needs.
Sore nipples usually mean she isn't taking enough of the breast into her mouth. Would you like me to help you try a different position at her next feed?
Whatever you decide about feeding, we'll support you. Would it help if someone from the infant feeding team came to see you today?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Supporting a mother with early breastfeeding difficulties on the postnatal ward
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Initiative standards and WHO breastfeeding guidance; assessment of feeding, weight monitoring and escalation follow local maternity and infant-feeding policies
core_concepts: Perceived insufficient milk and nipple pain are among the commonest reasons mothers stop breastfeeding in the first week, and both are often addressable.
Frequent feeding and cluster feeding are normal in the first days and help establish milk supply.
Support must be non-judgemental: the mother's informed choice is respected, including a choice to give formula.
diagnostic_clues: Pain throughout the feed and a baby attached mainly to the nipple suggest shallow attachment.
Expected wet and dirty nappies and a normal baby check are reassuring signs of adequate intake at this stage.
common_misconceptions: A baby who feeds very often must be hungry because there is not enough milk.
Breastfeeding is supposed to hurt at first and nothing can be done.
Encouraging breastfeeding means discouraging any discussion of formula.
dangerous_errors: Dismissing real warning signs of poor intake (few wet nappies, a very sleepy baby who will not feed, jaundice, signs of dehydration) instead of escalating to the midwife or doctor.
Pressuring or shaming the mother about her feeding choice.
Telling her the pain will go away by itself without looking at attachment.
management_principles: Explore the mother's experience and emotions first, then give accurate, chunked information.
Offer practical, hands-on help with position and attachment and involve the infant feeding team.
Explain the signs of effective feeding, check understanding, and respect her decision.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Expected nappy counts, weight-check timing and acceptable weight loss thresholds vary by local protocol; follow maternity policy.
Babies with jaundice, poor feeding, excessive sleepiness or significant weight loss need midwife or medical review, not reassurance alone.
Role boundaries between nurses, midwives and infant-feeding specialists differ between countries and units.
